entries.mechanism: Repeated, varied, meaningful encounters with definitions plus contexts build depth of word knowledge that incidental exposure delivers too slowly.
constraints: Effects on taught words far exceed effects on standardized measures
The number of words teachable directly is limited
Word depth, not just breadth, is the target
risks: Word lists without meaningful use
Expecting standardized comprehension gains from a short programme
Choosing rare words with low utility

observableEvidence.measure: Researcher-designed measures of the taught words plus observed spontaneous use, reported separately from standardized measures
observableEvidence.caveat: Standardized measures will understate the taught-word effect and should not be conflated

evidence.basis: Meta-analysis shows large effects on researcher-developed measures of taught words and much smaller effects on standardized measures.
evidence.generalizability: Preschool and early primary, including multilingual learners.

effect.note: Researcher-developed measures; roughly 0.29 on standardized measures.

recommendation.rationale: Teach high-utility words explicitly, and report taught-word and standardized outcomes separately so the effect is not overstated.

entries.label: Elaborative interrogation
entries.summary: Prompt the learner to explain why a stated fact is true, linking it to what they already know.
entries.mechanism: Generating a reason integrates the new fact with existing knowledge and exposes gaps that passive reading leaves hidden.
prerequisites: Some relevant prior knowledge to elaborate from
constraints: Benefits shrink when prior knowledge is very low
Not applicable to arbitrary associations
Learner-generated explanations may be wrong and need checking
risks: Accepting fluent but incorrect explanations
Using it for arbitrary facts where no reason exists
Adding time without checking the elaboration's accuracy

observableEvidence.measure: Coding of explanation correctness plus delayed factual and inference tests
observableEvidence.caveat: Verbose explanations are not better explanations

evidence.basis: Rated moderate utility in a comprehensive evidence review; benefits established mainly for factual material with existing prior knowledge.
evidence.generalizability: Mostly laboratory and short classroom studies with factual content.

recommendation.rationale: Cheap addition for explainable facts; verify the generated explanation rather than assuming it.

entries.label: Engagement: behavioural, emotional, and cognitive
entries.summary: Engagement is a multidimensional construct, and behavioural on-task appearance is the weakest of its three dimensions as evidence of learning.
entries.mechanism: Behaviour, affect, and cognitive investment vary independently, so a compliant learner can be cognitively disengaged and vice versa.
prerequisites: Measures that distinguish the three dimensions
constraints: Behavioural proxies dominate available data and are the least informative
Definitions vary widely across studies
Engagement metrics are easy to optimize without learning
risks: Optimizing time-in-app as an educational outcome
Reading compliance as cognitive engagement
Penalizing learners for disengagement caused by the design

observableEvidence.measure: Explanation quality and self-regulated strategy use alongside behavioural logs
observableEvidence.caveat: Click and time metrics measure the product, not the learning

evidence.basis: A widely adopted three-dimensional synthesis; the constituent measures vary substantially in quality.
evidence.generalizability: Broad conceptual adoption; measurement quality is the weak point.

recommendation.rationale: Never report a single engagement number; separate the dimensions and treat behavioural data as the weakest signal.

entries.label: Errorful learning and the hypercorrection effect
entries.summary: Errors made with feedback support learning, and confidently held errors are especially likely to be corrected and stay corrected.
entries.mechanism: An error creates a discrepancy that draws attention to the feedback; high-confidence errors produce surprise, which enhances encoding of the correction.
prerequisites: Feedback that actually follows the error
constraints: Without feedback, errors can persist
The benefit is about learning, not about arranging failure for its own sake
Public error exposure carries social cost
risks: Designing for failure without guaranteeing correction
Exposing errors publicly in unsafe climates
Assuming error rate itself is a goal

observableEvidence.measure: Track error, confidence, feedback, and later retention of the correction
observableEvidence.caveat: Uncorrected errors are consolidated by the same mechanism

evidence.basis: A well-replicated body of experiments, reviewed comprehensively, showing errors followed by feedback benefit learning and that high-confidence errors are corrected most readily.
evidence.generalizability: Broad across ages and materials where feedback is provided.

recommendation.rationale: Design for errors plus guaranteed correction and safety; never for errors alone.

entries.label: Executive-function curricula and training programmes
entries.summary: Curricula designed to build self-regulation show mixed results: some trials report meaningful gains, others null effects, and far transfer to achievement is not reliable.
entries.mechanism: Structured play and regulation routines are intended to give repeated practice at inhibition and planning within classroom activity.
constraints: Results vary sharply across trials and sites
Effects are largest where baseline regulation support was weakest
Implementation fidelity explains much of the variance
risks: Adopting a branded curriculum on early promising results
Assuming EF gains produce achievement gains
Displacing language and content learning

observableEvidence.indicator: Regulation and academic outcomes reported separately
observableEvidence.measure: Direct EF measures plus independent academic measures with fidelity data
observableEvidence.timing: Across a programme year and after
observableEvidence.caveat: Positive EF results do not imply academic results

evidence.basis: Randomized trials of the best-known curriculum show inconsistent results across sites, and the broader review finds transfer is narrow.
evidence.generalizability: Preschool and early primary; site-dependent.

recommendation.rationale: Treat as a local experiment with fidelity monitoring and separate reporting of regulation and academic outcomes.

entries.label: Executive function development
aliases: inhibitory control, working memory, cognitive flexibility
entries.summary: Inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility develop through childhood, predict school outcomes, and are supported by repeated challenge in meaningful activity.
entries.mechanism: These capacities improve with sustained practice at the edge of current ability, embedded in activities the child cares about and with adult support for emotional and physical state.
prerequisites: Activities that repeatedly stress the target capacity
constraints: Transfer is narrow: gains appear on trained and near skills
Stress, sleep, and physical state substantially affect performance
Age norms describe groups, not individuals
risks: Buying commercial EF training expecting academic gains
Diagnosing individuals from age norms
Treating dysregulation as defiance

observableEvidence.measure: Direct EF tasks plus observation in real classroom demands
observableEvidence.caveat: Laboratory task gains rarely generalize to classroom behaviour

evidence.basis: Comprehensive reviews establish the construct, its developmental course, and the narrowness of transfer from training.
evidence.generalizability: Well established for early and middle childhood.

recommendation.rationale: Support executive function inside meaningful activity; expect narrow transfer and never diagnose from age norms.

entries.label: Expectancy-value theory of achievement motivation
entries.summary: Choice, persistence, and performance depend jointly on expectancy of success and on subjective task value, minus perceived cost.
entries.mechanism: Learners act where they expect to succeed and where the task carries interest, utility, or identity value at acceptable cost; either term at zero collapses engagement.
prerequisites: A measurable expectancy and value profile
A task the learner can actually choose to engage or not
constraints: Cost is often the neglected and decisive term
Values are situated and change with context and identity
Self-report measures dominate the evidence
risks: Treating low effort as low ability when it is low value or high cost
Raising expectancy with false reassurance
Ignoring opportunity cost for working adults

observableEvidence.measure: Validated scales plus observed choice and persistence
observableEvidence.caveat: Stated value can shift quickly with early success or failure

evidence.basis: Decades of longitudinal and experimental work consolidated in a major theoretical review; the cited evidence is a theory synthesis plus intervention studies rather than a pooled effect synthesis.
evidence.generalizability: Broad across ages and domains; measurement is self-report heavy.
evidence.notes: Graded context-dependent under the 0.2.0 rule that a strong grade must rest on a synthesis-grade source; the theory is well supported, the cited base is not a synthesis of effects.

recommendation.rationale: Diagnose disengagement by separating expectancy, value, and cost before attributing it to effort.

entries.label: Expertise reversal effect
aliases: instructional method by prior knowledge interaction
entries.summary: Instructional support that helps novices becomes redundant and then harmful as learners gain knowledge, so guidance must be faded against measured expertise.
entries.mechanism: Once a learner holds the relevant schema, external guidance must be reconciled with internal knowledge, adding processing that serves no purpose.
prerequisites: A measure of current domain-specific prior knowledge
The ability to change support level
constraints: Expertise is knowledge-component specific, not a global learner level
Requires ongoing measurement, not a one-time placement
Reversal points differ by task and by learner
risks: Freezing support at the novice setting for a whole course
Using a global 'level' label instead of task-specific evidence
Fading support faster than competence grows

observableEvidence.indicator: Interaction of support level with prior knowledge
observableEvidence.measure: Compare supported and unsupported conditions across prior-knowledge bands
observableEvidence.caveat: An average effect hides the interaction that matters

evidence.basis: A replicated interaction documented across many instructional-design experiments and syntheses.
evidence.generalizability: Well evidenced in well-structured domains; the reversal point is task-specific.

recommendation.rationale: The single most important boundary condition on scaffolding, worked examples, and multimedia guidance; enforce it as a fading rule.

entries.label: Explicit instruction (principles of instruction)
entries.summary: Present new material in small steps with modelling, guided practice, high-frequency questioning, checks for understanding, and independent practice.
entries.mechanism: Small steps and frequent checks keep working-memory demand manageable and surface errors before they are practised, while modelling makes expert processes visible.
prerequisites: A decomposable skill or body of knowledge
Time for guided then independent practice
constraints: Explicit is not lecture: it requires high-frequency response and checking
Guidance must fade as competence grows
Weakest fit for open, ill-structured, or judgment-laden tasks
risks: Degenerating into uninterrupted teacher talk
Holding guidance constant past the point of expertise reversal
Over-fitting to the taught examples with no varied practice

observableEvidence.measure: Check-for-understanding hit rate during the lesson plus unassisted delayed items
observableEvidence.timing: Within lesson and after a delay
observableEvidence.caveat: High choral response can mask individual non-understanding

evidence.basis: Synthesis of process-product research, cognitive-science findings, and expert-teacher studies converging on the same set of practices; strongest for foundational and well-structured content.
evidence.generalizability: Broad for well-structured content and novice learners; weaker evidence for open-ended disciplinary work.

recommendation.rationale: Sound default for novel well-structured content, provided checking is frequent and guidance fades.

entries.label: External focus of attention in motor learning
aliases: focus on the effect not the body
entries.summary: Instructions that direct attention to the movement's external effect produce better motor performance and learning than instructions focused on body movements.
entries.mechanism: An external focus permits automatic control processes to operate, while an internal focus induces conscious interference with them.
prerequisites: An identifiable external effect to focus on
Cue wording that is genuinely external
constraints: Effects vary by skill and expertise level
Much of the evidence is short-term laboratory work
Wording distinctions are subtle and often mis-implemented
risks: Cues that are labelled external but describe the body
Assuming it applies to every skill and stage
Overgeneralizing from single-session studies

observableEvidence.indicator: Performance and retention by cue type
observableEvidence.measure: Matched tasks with internal versus external cue wording plus delayed retention
observableEvidence.caveat: Coaches routinely misclassify their own cues

evidence.basis: A substantial review reporting consistent advantages for external focus, though largely from short laboratory studies.
evidence.generalizability: Motor tasks across ages; durability evidence is thinner.

recommendation.rationale: Cheap cue-wording change worth adopting; verify cues are genuinely external and measure retention.

entries.label: Basic fact fluency and automaticity
entries.summary: Building efficient retrieval of basic facts frees working memory for multi-step reasoning, but fluency work must follow understanding and avoid anxiety-inducing formats.
entries.mechanism: Automatic retrieval removes the working-memory cost of recomputing components inside a larger problem.
prerequisites: Conceptual understanding of the operation first
constraints: Timed public drills are a documented anxiety source
Fluency is a means to reasoning, not the goal
Strategy-based fluency outperforms rote drill for many learners
risks: Timed tests entrenching mathematics anxiety
Fluency work before understanding
Confusing speed with mathematical competence

observableEvidence.measure: Fluency probes plus performance on multi-step problems and an anxiety check
observableEvidence.caveat: Faster facts alone do not indicate better mathematics

evidence.basis: Evidence-rated intervention guidance recommends fluency-building activities, while the anxiety literature constrains the format.
evidence.generalizability: Primary and middle grades, especially learners with mathematics difficulty.

sourceLocators.locator: Recommendation on building fluent retrieval of basic arithmetic facts

recommendation.rationale: Build fluency after understanding, in short distributed low-stakes sessions rather than timed public drills.

entries.label: Feedback levels: task, process, self-regulation, and self
entries.summary: Feedback about the task, the process, and self-regulation supports learning, while feedback about the person is ineffective or harmful.
entries.mechanism: Feedback works by reducing a gap between current and desired understanding; person-directed feedback carries no gap-closing information and diverts attention to the self.
prerequisites: A clear goal the learner understands
An opportunity to act on it
constraints: A substantial minority of feedback interventions reduce performance
Praise directed at the person does not improve learning
Feedback without a chance to revise is inert
risks: Grades crowding out attention to comments
Person praise creating contingent self-worth
Overwhelming volume of correction

observableEvidence.measure: Evidence of the feedback being acted on plus performance on the next attempt
observableEvidence.caveat: Reading feedback is not acting on it

evidence.basis: Convergent evidence from the classic feedback meta-analysis, the four-level synthesis, and later meta-analyses of feedback in education.
evidence.generalizability: Broad; effect sign depends on level and on revision opportunity.

effect.note: Average positive effect with wide variance; over a third of interventions in the classic meta-analysis reduced performance.

recommendation.rationale: Direct feedback at task, process, or self-regulation, and always provide the revision opportunity that makes it usable.

entries.label: Feedback uptake and learner feedback literacy
entries.summary: Feedback only counts when the learner appreciates, judges, and acts on it, so systems must design for uptake rather than for delivery.
entries.mechanism: Learners need the capability to evaluate quality, manage the affective response, and take action; without it, well-formed comments produce nothing.
prerequisites: A subsequent task where the feedback applies
Exemplars and criteria the learner can use to judge quality
constraints: Uptake capability must be developed deliberately
Emotional response mediates use
Evidence base is largely conceptual and higher-education-based
risks: Measuring feedback quality by volume produced
Assuming uptake because comments were delivered
Blaming learners for not using feedback they were never taught to use

observableEvidence.measure: Comparison of successive drafts or attempts plus learner accounts of what they changed
observableEvidence.caveat: Satisfaction with feedback correlates weakly with using it

evidence.basis: A conceptual framework with growing but largely qualitative higher-education evidence; consistent with the finding that feedback needs a revision opportunity.
evidence.generalizability: Mostly higher education; limited causal evidence.

recommendation.rationale: Design the uptake step explicitly and measure the change it produced, not the feedback delivered.

entries.label: Flipped classroom
entries.summary: Moving first exposure before class and using class time for practice and feedback yields a small positive average effect on learning.
entries.mechanism: Class time is reallocated from transmission to guided practice with feedback; the gain depends on what actually fills the reclaimed time.
prerequisites: Reliable pre-class access for every learner
A designed in-class activity, not free time
constraints: The effect comes from the in-class redesign, not the video
Adding pre-class work without removing anything increases total load
Access inequities directly become learning inequities
risks: Assuming video watching happened
Doubling workload rather than reallocating it
Widening gaps for learners without home connectivity

observableEvidence.indicator: Learning versus the same course unflipped
observableEvidence.measure: Common assessments plus pre-class completion and in-class activity records
observableEvidence.caveat: Satisfaction ratings often drop even when learning rises

evidence.basis: Meta-analysis finds a small positive average effect on learning with no consistent satisfaction advantage; quizzing on pre-class material is a positive moderator.
evidence.generalizability: Mostly higher education and secondary; heterogeneous designs.

effect.note: Small positive effect on learning outcomes; near-zero on student satisfaction.

recommendation.rationale: Worthwhile only if the reclaimed class time is redesigned for practice and feedback and access is guaranteed.

entries.label: Formative assessment as an adaptive cycle
entries.summary: Elicit evidence, interpret it against a learning goal, and change the next learner or instructional action.
entries.mechanism: A valid short-cycle signal reduces uncertainty about the current gap and makes feedback, regrouping, reteaching, or learner revision responsive.
prerequisites: Clear learning goal and success criteria
An elicitation aligned to the construct
constraints: The cycle is formative only if evidence changes a next action
Keep interpretations proportional to evidence
risks: Calling any quiz formative
Collecting dashboards without adaptation
Repeating broad effect-size claims across heterogeneous implementations

observableEvidence.indicator: Evidence-contingent next action and gap closure
observableEvidence.measure: Documented regrouping, reteaching, feedback uptake, revision, and follow-up task
observableEvidence.caveat: The existence of a score or quiz is not evidence of formative use

evidence.basis: Influential positive review plus a critical review documenting definition, implementation, and magnitude problems.
evidence.generalizability: Broad logic; effects depend heavily on domain, implementation, population, and follow-through.

recommendation.rationale: Retrieve the full evidence-to-action loop, not an assessment event in isolation.

entries.label: Formative assessment effect size caution
entries.summary: Formative assessment is widely endorsed, but rigorous meta-analytic estimates of its effect are much smaller than the figures commonly quoted, and vary by what was actually implemented.
entries.mechanism: The label covers everything from a five-minute exit ticket to a whole-school system, so pooled estimates aggregate incomparable interventions.
prerequisites: A specific described practice rather than the umbrella label
constraints: Widely cited large effect figures are not supported by later rigorous syntheses
Effects vary by subject, format, and implementation
Publication and implementation quality vary widely
risks: Marketing an inflated effect size
Treating any quizzing as formative assessment
Abandoning the practice because the headline number shrank

observableEvidence.indicator: Specified practice with its own evidence
observableEvidence.measure: Describe the exact practice and cite evidence for that practice, not the umbrella term
observableEvidence.timing: At the point of any claim
observableEvidence.caveat: Umbrella-label effect sizes are uninterpretable

evidence.basis: A rigorous meta-analysis produced substantially smaller estimates than the widely quoted earlier figures, and a critical review documented conceptual imprecision in the construct.
evidence.generalizability: The caution applies wherever the umbrella term is used.

effect.note: Approximate meta-analytic estimate, well below the often-quoted 0.4 to 0.7 range.

recommendation.rationale: Name the specific practice and cite its own evidence; never quote an umbrella formative-assessment effect size.

entries.label: Serious games and game-based learning
entries.summary: Well-designed instructional games can improve learning modestly relative to conventional instruction, especially when supplemented with other instruction and played over multiple sessions.
entries.mechanism: Games provide continuous responding, immediate consequence feedback, and goal structures, but only the instructionally aligned parts produce learning.
prerequisites: Alignment of game mechanics with the target knowledge
constraints: Effects depend on design, not on being a game
Motivation gains do not reliably follow
Off-task play consumes time invisibly
risks: Assuming engagement equals learning
Mechanics that reward speed over reasoning
Buying a game and skipping the surrounding instruction

observableEvidence.measure: Transfer assessment outside the game environment plus time-on-task logs
observableEvidence.caveat: In-game scores mostly measure game skill

evidence.basis: Meta-analyses find small-to-moderate learning advantages over conventional instruction, moderated by supplementary instruction and number of sessions; motivation effects are not consistent.
evidence.generalizability: Heterogeneous across genres, ages, and subjects.

effect.note: Learning advantage over conventional instruction; motivation effects not reliably positive.

recommendation.rationale: Judge the instructional design, not the format; require an out-of-game transfer measure.

entries.label: Gamification of non-game learning activities
entries.summary: Adding game elements such as points, badges, and leaderboards to ordinary activities produces small positive effects on cognitive and behavioural outcomes and is highly design-dependent.
entries.mechanism: Game elements can add goal clarity and progress feedback; competitive elements can also crowd out interest and disadvantage lower performers.
prerequisites: An activity that is worth doing repeatedly
Progress signals tied to real learning, not clicks
constraints: Effects are small and vary by element type
Public leaderboards can harm lower-performing learners
Extrinsic rewards can undermine existing intrinsic interest
risks: Optimizing streaks and points over understanding
Ranking learners publicly
Manufacturing compliance and calling it motivation

observableEvidence.measure: Learning outcomes plus voluntary return after rewards stop, disaggregated by performance band
observableEvidence.timing: During and after removal of the mechanics
observableEvidence.caveat: Engagement metrics rise most for those already succeeding

evidence.basis: Meta-analysis finds small positive average effects on cognitive, motivational, and behavioural outcomes with strong dependence on which elements are used.
evidence.generalizability: Broad but element-specific; competitive elements are the riskiest.

effect.note: Cognitive outcomes; motivational and behavioural effects smaller.

recommendation.rationale: Prefer progress and mastery signals over competition; check effects for the lowest-performing band separately.

entries.label: Generation effect
entries.summary: Information a learner generates is remembered better than the same information read, provided generation succeeds or is corrected.
entries.mechanism: Generating engages the retrieval and construction processes that later recall depends on, creating a stronger and more distinctive trace.
constraints: Fails without adequate prior knowledge or feedback
Effect sizes are modest for complex material
Time cost per item is higher than reading
risks: Uncorrected generation consolidating errors
Applying it to material with no basis for generation
Confusing it with unguided discovery of new concepts

observableEvidence.indicator: Recall for generated versus read items
observableEvidence.measure: Within-subject item comparison at delay
observableEvidence.caveat: Generation is slower per item; compare per unit time as well

evidence.basis: A classic and widely replicated memory effect, with modern reviews clarifying that errorful generation also helps when feedback follows.
evidence.generalizability: Robust for verbal material; smaller and more conditional for complex content.

recommendation.rationale: Prefer generation over presentation whenever feedback can immediately follow.

entries.label: Gesture and embodied representation
entries.summary: Producing and observing task-relevant gestures supports learning of spatial and relational content and can make emerging understanding visible.
entries.mechanism: Gesture externalizes spatial and relational structure, offloads working memory, and expresses knowledge a learner cannot yet verbalize.
prerequisites: Content with spatial or relational structure
A gesture that maps to that structure
constraints: Arbitrary gestures do not help
Evidence is strongest for children and spatial or mathematical content
Accessibility alternatives are needed for learners who cannot see or produce gestures
risks: Adding decorative movement
Requiring gesture in ways that exclude some learners
Reading gesture as proficiency

observableEvidence.measure: Coded gesture during explanation plus post-instruction performance
observableEvidence.caveat: Mismatch signals readiness, not mastery

evidence.basis: Experimental work shows gesture production causally aids learning of mathematical and spatial content and reveals transitional knowledge.
evidence.generalizability: Strongest for children learning spatial or mathematical relations.

recommendation.rationale: Use structurally meaningful gesture for spatial and relational content, with accessible alternatives available.

entries.label: Specific goals and implementation intentions
entries.summary: Specific, difficult, accepted goals outperform vague ones, and if-then plans that specify when and where to act close much of the intention-action gap.
entries.mechanism: Specific goals direct attention and effort and permit self-monitoring; if-then plans delegate initiation to a situational cue rather than to willpower.
prerequisites: The skill to actually perform the action
constraints: Specific difficult goals harm performance on tasks still being learned
Goals without feedback do little
They can narrow attention and encourage gaming the metric
risks: Setting outcome goals for skills not yet acquired
Metric fixation and neglect of unmeasured goals
Demoralization when goals are imposed rather than accepted

observableEvidence.measure: Rate of intended action performed plus progress on the target skill
observableEvidence.caveat: Goal attainment can be met by lowering the standard

evidence.basis: One of the most replicated findings in organizational psychology, with a large separate literature on implementation intentions.
evidence.generalizability: Robust for performance of acquired skills; weaker or negative during acquisition.

effect.note: Implementation-intention effects on goal attainment are typically medium-to-large.

recommendation.rationale: Use learning goals during acquisition and performance goals after; always pair with progress feedback.

entries.label: Grit as a predictor
aliases: perseverance and passion for long-term goals
entries.summary: Grit adds little predictive power beyond conscientiousness, and its perseverance facet does nearly all the work.
entries.mechanism: The measure largely re-describes conscientiousness; the passion-for-consistency facet contributes minimally to prediction.
prerequisites: None; the construct is being assessed rather than applied
constraints: Incremental validity over conscientiousness is small
Correlations with performance are modest
There is no evidence base for durable grit training
risks: Using grit scores in selection or placement
Attributing structural barriers to insufficient perseverance
Selling grit curricula as evidence-based

observableEvidence.measure: Hierarchical regression including conscientiousness, not grit alone
observableEvidence.caveat: Zero-order correlations look far more impressive than incremental ones

evidence.basis: Meta-analysis finds grit is strongly correlated with conscientiousness, weakly predictive of performance, and largely reducible to its perseverance facet.
evidence.generalizability: Broad; the critique is measurement-level.

effect.note: Approximate meta-analytic correlation with academic performance; minimal incremental validity over conscientiousness.

recommendation.rationale: Do not use as a selection variable or as a target of instruction; treat persistence as situational and supportable.

entries.label: Growth-mindset intervention warning
entries.summary: Do not treat brief growth-mindset messaging as a general achievement intervention or replacement for strategy, instruction, feedback, and opportunity.
entries.mechanism: The proposed path from malleability belief to challenge seeking and effort is plausible, but changing a belief does not itself supply knowledge, effective strategy, or resources.
prerequisites: If used, pair with effective strategies and structural support
Pre-register objective outcomes and manipulation checks
constraints: Separate belief change from achievement effects
risks: Praising effort without effective strategy
Blaming learners
Replacing instruction or resources with slogans

observableEvidence.indicator: Behavior and achievement beyond self-reported belief
observableEvidence.measure: Challenge choice, strategy change, persistence, and long-term objective outcome
observableEvidence.caveat: A successful mindset manipulation is not an achievement effect

evidence.basis: Large critical meta-analysis found tiny overall effects and nonsignificant effects in higher-quality or bias-adjusted subsets.
evidence.generalizability: Does not support a general achievement intervention claim.

recommendation.rationale: At most a small contextual component; never a substitute for substantive teaching and opportunity.

entries.label: Guided inquiry and guided discovery
entries.summary: Inquiry works when it is guided: unassisted discovery underperforms, while inquiry with explicit guidance, feedback, and worked support outperforms both.
entries.mechanism: Guidance keeps search within a productive space so learners test ideas rather than exhaust working memory on unconstrained exploration.
prerequisites: Explicit guidance, prompts, or worked support
constraints: The amount of guidance, not the inquiry label, drives the effect
Younger and lower-prior-knowledge learners need more guidance
Teacher-led inquiry activities show larger effects than pure student-led ones
risks: Equating inquiry with minimal guidance
Confirming misconceptions through unguided exploration
Assessing enthusiasm instead of understanding

observableEvidence.indicator: Concept and epistemic gains under specified guidance
observableEvidence.measure: Concept measures plus records of what guidance was actually provided
observableEvidence.caveat: Guidance level is often unreported, making results uninterpretable

evidence.basis: Meta-analyses consistently show unassisted discovery underperforms explicit instruction while guided discovery outperforms both; guidance is the decisive moderator.
evidence.generalizability: Robust across ages and science topics.

effect.note: Enhanced/guided discovery versus other conditions; unassisted discovery is negative relative to explicit instruction.

recommendation.rationale: Adopt inquiry only with specified guidance; record the guidance level as part of the design.

entries.label: Guided play
entries.summary: Combine genuine child choice and meaningful play with a clear learning goal and responsive adult questions, hints, modeling, or environment design.
entries.mechanism: Agency and exploration sustain engagement while contingent guidance focuses attention on relevant relations.
constraints: Evidence is narrow and heterogeneous
Preserve the distinction from free play and scripted direct instruction
risks: Calling any playful-looking worksheet guided play
Assuming superiority for all literacy, social-emotional, or executive-function outcomes

observableEvidence.indicator: Child-led exploration focused by adaptive guidance
observableEvidence.measure: Choice, prompt contingency, persistence, explanation, and target-domain outcome
observableEvidence.timing: During play and on a separate target check
observableEvidence.caveat: Enjoyment alone does not show concept learning

evidence.basis: Systematic review found benefits for some early math, shape, and switching outcomes, often from few studies, and nulls elsewhere.
evidence.generalizability: Mainly ages one to eight; strongest for selected early mathematics and spatial outcomes.

recommendation.rationale: Retrieve with an explicit target, real child agency, responsive guidance, and domain-specific measurement.

entries.label: Historical thinking: sourcing, contextualizing, corroborating
entries.summary: Teaching learners to source, contextualize, and corroborate documents improves historical reasoning and can also improve general reading comprehension.
entries.mechanism: Attending to who produced a text, when, and why converts reading from information extraction into evidence evaluation.
prerequisites: Curated document sets with real interpretive tension
constraints: Requires substantial background knowledge to contextualize
Expert heuristics do not appear spontaneously in novices
Curriculum time cost is significant
risks: Document activities without background knowledge
Reducing history to generic critical thinking
Assuming digital source evaluation transfers automatically

observableEvidence.indicator: Use of sourcing heuristics on new documents
observableEvidence.measure: Coded think-aloud or written analysis of unfamiliar documents
observableEvidence.timing: After the unit and at delay
observableEvidence.caveat: Naming the heuristic is not using it

evidence.basis: Classic expert-novice studies plus classroom intervention evidence showing gains in historical thinking and some transfer to general comprehension.
evidence.generalizability: Secondary history classrooms, mostly United States studies.

recommendation.rationale: Strong fit for evidence-based reasoning goals; guarantee the background knowledge the contextualizing step requires.

entries.label: Home learning environment and family practices
entries.summary: Informal exposure to literacy and formal teaching of skills at home predict different outcomes: shared reading predicts vocabulary, direct teaching predicts early decoding.
entries.mechanism: Different home activities provide different inputs; meaning-focused exposure builds language while explicit teaching builds code skills.
prerequisites: Materials and time available in the home
Guidance in the home's own language
constraints: Largely correlational with substantial confounding
Home practices vary by culture and resources, and difference is not deficit
Effects are activity-specific, not a general involvement factor
risks: Deficit framing of families
Assigning school-like homework to families as a fix
Assuming one home activity improves all outcomes

observableEvidence.measure: Distinguish exposure and teaching activities and link each to matched child measures
observableEvidence.caveat: A global involvement score hides which activity did the work

evidence.basis: Longitudinal work distinguishing informal and formal home literacy experiences with differentiated outcome prediction; evidence is correlational.
evidence.generalizability: Demonstrated across several languages; culturally situated.

recommendation.rationale: Support specific activities matched to specific goals, in the family's language, without deficit framing.

entries.label: Homework as distributed practice
entries.summary: Homework's association with achievement is near zero in primary school and grows with age; the quality and purpose of the task matters more than the amount.
entries.mechanism: Out-of-class work can provide spacing and retrieval, but only if the task is practicable independently and errors are corrected afterwards.
prerequisites: The learner can do it without help
constraints: Age moderates the association strongly
Correlational evidence dominates; causal claims are weak
Home resource inequality is directly transmitted into outcomes
risks: Assigning new material as homework
Amplifying inequity between home environments
Uncorrected practice consolidating errors

observableEvidence.measure: Completion without assistance plus delayed in-class retrieval performance
observableEvidence.caveat: Completion rate says nothing about who did it

evidence.basis: Synthesis of largely correlational studies showing a strong age gradient and dependence on task design.
evidence.generalizability: Association near zero for young children, moderate for secondary.

effect.note: Effectively zero in elementary grades; increasing through secondary school.

recommendation.rationale: Justify each assignment by spacing or retrieval purpose; never assign unlearned material, and check equity of home conditions.

entries.label: ICAP cognitive-engagement ordering
entries.summary: Classify overt engagement as passive, active, constructive, or interactive and predict deeper learning when learners generate beyond given information or co-construct reasoning.
entries.mechanism: Generative activity creates new inferences; substantive dialogue can expose and jointly repair gaps beyond each participant's initial contribution.
constraints: Overt activity is only a proxy for cognitive engagement
The predicted ordering has caveats and depends on activity quality
risks: Calling clicks active learning
Assuming any group work is interactive
Maximizing activity at the expense of knowledge or clarity

observableEvidence.measure: Quality and novelty of notes, explanations, maps, dialogue uptake, and delayed learning
observableEvidence.timing: During activity and on independent follow-up
observableEvidence.caveat: Behavioral category alone does not establish mechanism or learning

evidence.basis: Theory article integrates laboratory and classroom evidence but states an ordering hypothesis with limitations, not a universal causal law.
evidence.generalizability: Useful as an activity-audit lens; effects depend on domain, prompt, and interaction quality.

recommendation.rationale: Use to formulate observable design predictions and compare outcomes, not to rank every activity mechanically.

entries.label: Explicit instruction in second language acquisition
entries.summary: Explicit second-language instruction outperforms purely implicit exposure, and effects are durable, though measurement type strongly shapes apparent size.
entries.mechanism: Explicit attention to form helps learners notice features that comprehensible input alone leaves unnoticed, especially for non-salient structures.
prerequisites: Meaningful input and output opportunities alongside form focus
Targets that benefit from explicit attention
constraints: Effects are inflated by constrained response measures over free production
Explicit instruction complements rather than replaces meaningful use
Durability evidence is limited to available delayed post-tests
risks: Grammar teaching with no communicative use
Judging success only on discrete-point tests
Assuming exposure alone suffices

observableEvidence.measure: Free constructed response alongside constrained measures
observableEvidence.caveat: Constrained measures overstate the effect substantially

evidence.basis: Landmark meta-analysis of instructed second-language acquisition showing large explicit-instruction advantages, moderated heavily by outcome measure type.
evidence.generalizability: Broad across languages and ages studied.

effect.note: Large average effects for explicit over implicit instruction, substantially smaller on free-response measures.

recommendation.rationale: Combine explicit form focus with meaningful use, and always report free-production outcomes.

entries.label: Instructional coaching for practitioners
entries.summary: Individualized, sustained coaching improves practice and, more modestly, learner outcomes; effects shrink substantially as programmes scale.
entries.mechanism: Observation plus individualized feedback on real practice closes the gap that workshop-based training leaves between knowing and doing.
constraints: Effects on learner outcomes are much smaller than on practice
Larger programmes show markedly smaller effects
Coach quality is the binding constraint at scale
risks: Scaling and expecting pilot-sized effects
Coaching used as evaluation, which destroys trust
One-off workshops labelled as coaching

observableEvidence.indicator: Practice change and learner outcomes, separately
observableEvidence.measure: Observation-rubric change plus independent learner achievement, with programme size reported
observableEvidence.caveat: Effects at pilot scale do not survive scaling

evidence.basis: Meta-analysis of teacher coaching finds large effects on instructional practice and smaller effects on achievement, with a clear scale-down pattern.
evidence.generalizability: Teacher development; the scaling caution is well documented.

effect.note: Effect on instructional practice; about 0.18 on student achievement, and smaller in larger programmes.

recommendation.rationale: Best-evidenced professional learning model; plan explicitly for the effect decay that comes with scale.

entries.label: Intelligent tutoring systems
entries.summary: Software that tracks a learner model at step granularity and gives step-level guidance performs close to human tutoring and well above untutored practice.
entries.mechanism: Step-level feedback and hints operate at the granularity where the learner's error actually occurs, giving frequent interaction opportunities that answer-level systems miss.
prerequisites: A domain decomposable into steps and knowledge components
A learner model and validated hint content
Classroom integration and teacher use of the data
constraints: Effects are strongest in well-structured domains
Interaction granularity matters more than the underlying AI technique
Implementation and teacher use explain much of the variance
risks: Optimizing for in-session correctness rather than delayed learning
Hint abuse and gaming the system
Assuming a chat interface delivers step-level tutoring without a learner model

observableEvidence.measure: Randomized or matched comparison on delayed independent assessment, plus hint-use and gaming detectors
observableEvidence.caveat: In-system mastery flags routinely overstate durable learning

evidence.basis: Convergent meta-analyses find ITS substantially better than no tutoring and roughly comparable to human tutoring, with step granularity as the key moderator.
evidence.generalizability: Well-structured domains, mostly mathematics, physics, and programming.

effect.note: Meta-analytic estimates versus conventional instruction commonly fall between 0.4 and 0.8.

recommendation.rationale: The most directly relevant precedent for an agentic tutoring runtime; the evidence is about step-level interaction, not about the technology label.

entries.label: Four-phase interest development
entries.summary: Interest develops from triggered situational interest through maintained situational interest into emerging and then well-developed individual interest, each phase needing different support.
entries.mechanism: Early phases depend on external triggers and meaningfulness; later phases are self-sustained by stored knowledge and value, so support must shift as interest deepens.
prerequisites: A trigger with genuine content connection
constraints: Triggering is easy; maintaining is the hard part
Novelty triggers fade and can distract from content
Phase assignment is inferential
risks: Using seductive details that trigger interest but harm learning
Assuming a triggered response indicates durable interest
Abandoning support once initial enthusiasm appears

observableEvidence.measure: Voluntary return, self-initiated questions, and knowledge growth over time
observableEvidence.caveat: One enthusiastic lesson is not interest development

evidence.basis: A well-articulated developmental model supported by correlational and design studies rather than by controlled phase-transition experiments.
evidence.generalizability: Broad conceptual use; causal evidence is limited.

recommendation.rationale: Match support to phase and measure voluntary re-engagement; do not count a trigger as an outcome.

entries.label: Interleaving for discrimination
entries.summary: Mix confusable categories or problem types so learners repeatedly choose the relevant concept or procedure.
entries.mechanism: Juxtaposition highlights discriminating features and practices strategy selection; part of the benefit may come from spacing.
prerequisites: Some initial knowledge of each category
Items whose comparison exposes a consequential distinction
constraints: Material type and similarity moderate outcomes
Blocked acquisition may precede mixed selection practice
risks: Universalizing from math or visual categories to prose or vocabulary
Mistaking lower practice performance for lower learning

observableEvidence.measure: Delayed classification, selected method, justification, and transfer
observableEvidence.caveat: Measure selection, not only execution after the category is named

evidence.basis: Meta-analysis finds a positive average with large material moderators, including null or reversed domains.
evidence.generalizability: Best supported for visual categories and mathematics; not general for expository text or word learning.

recommendation.rationale: Use when the target is discrimination among confusable types and learners have initial footholds.

entries.label: Background knowledge as a driver of comprehension
entries.summary: Topic knowledge substantially determines what a reader understands and remembers, and can outweigh general reading skill on knowledge-dependent texts.
entries.mechanism: Existing schemas fill inferential gaps that texts always leave, so a knowledgeable weak decoder can outperform a knowledge-poor strong decoder on that topic.
prerequisites: Texts that build on prior units
constraints: Comprehension is not a generic transferable skill
Standardized comprehension scores partly measure topic familiarity
Knowledge takes sustained curricular time to build
risks: Endless generic strategy practice in place of knowledge
Interpreting a comprehension score as a fixed reading ability
Assuming a topic-specific result generalizes

observableEvidence.measure: Same-format comprehension on familiar and unfamiliar topics
observableEvidence.caveat: A comprehension score is partly a knowledge score

evidence.basis: Classic experimental demonstration plus consistent findings in evidence-rated comprehension guidance emphasizing knowledge alongside strategies.
evidence.generalizability: Broad; the size of the knowledge advantage depends on how knowledge-dependent the text is.

recommendation.rationale: Build knowledge deliberately, and interpret comprehension scores as partly topic-dependent.

entries.label: Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (knowledge component) framework
entries.summary: Decompose a domain into knowledge components, then match each component's type to the learning process and instructional method that actually serves it.
entries.mechanism: Different component types (facts, rules, principles) are acquired by different processes (memory and fluency, induction and refinement, sense-making), so instruction should be chosen per component rather than per topic.
prerequisites: A way to attribute items to components
constraints: Component granularity is a modeling choice that changes conclusions
Poorly specified components produce confidently wrong learner models
Not every valued outcome decomposes cleanly
risks: Fragmenting a coherent practice into meaningless atoms
Treating a fitted model as the learner's actual mind
Optimizing component mastery while losing the whole task

observableEvidence.measure: Error rate by opportunity count per component, plus model fit comparison
observableEvidence.caveat: A good curve fit does not validate the component definition

evidence.basis: A well-specified framework with substantial supporting work in tutoring systems; it organizes evidence rather than being a single intervention effect.
evidence.generalizability: Best evidenced in well-structured domains such as mathematics and programming.

recommendation.rationale: The natural bridge from a knowledge rack to a working graph; adopt the decomposition discipline, and keep component definitions revisable.

entries.label: Corrective feedback in second-language learning
entries.summary: Corrective feedback benefits second-language accuracy, with explicit feedback showing larger immediate effects and implicit feedback holding up better over time.
entries.mechanism: Feedback marks a gap between output and target form; explicitness determines whether the learner notices it, while depth of processing affects durability.
constraints: Explicit and implicit forms show different time courses
Overcorrection can suppress production
Most studies are short-term with laboratory-like tasks
risks: Correcting every error and reducing willingness to speak
Judging by immediate post-test only
Ignoring learner affect in public correction

observableEvidence.measure: Reformulation rate plus delayed accuracy in free production
observableEvidence.caveat: Immediate uptake does not predict durable change

evidence.basis: Meta-analysis finds a medium overall effect for corrective feedback with a differential time course for explicit versus implicit types.
evidence.generalizability: Instructed second-language settings; mostly short interventions.

effect.note: Medium overall effect; explicit types larger immediately, implicit types more durable.

recommendation.rationale: Select feedback explicitness by target and stage, protect willingness to communicate, and measure at delay.

entries.label: Assuming learners are the best judges of their own instruction
entries.summary: Learners' preferences and self-assessments are poor guides to what will produce learning, because the conditions that feel best often produce the least durable results.
entries.mechanism: Preference tracks fluency and comfort, and the manipulations that improve long-term retention reliably reduce both during learning.
prerequisites: None; this is a screening criterion
constraints: Learner voice matters for legitimacy, access, and equity even where it is a poor guide to method effectiveness
The point concerns judgments of instructional effectiveness, not learners' rights or preferences generally
risks: Optimizing a product for satisfaction and losing learning
Dropping effective methods because ratings fell
Dismissing learner concerns about access and fairness by citing this finding

observableEvidence.measure: Course or product satisfaction alongside delayed independent learning measures
observableEvidence.caveat: The two can and do move in opposite directions

evidence.basis: Direct experimental demonstration that perceived learning diverges from measured learning, plus reviews of learner misjudgment of study effectiveness.
evidence.generalizability: Demonstrated in higher education and laboratory settings.

recommendation.rationale: Never use satisfaction as a learning metric; do continue to take learner voice seriously on access, fairness, and workload.

entries.label: Strategy selection by phase of learning
entries.summary: The effectiveness of a learning strategy depends on whether the learner is acquiring surface knowledge, consolidating deep relations, or attempting transfer.
entries.mechanism: Strategies that build initial representations differ from those that relate ideas or that cue application, so a strategy's average effect hides a phase interaction.
prerequisites: A judgment of the learner's current phase for this content
constraints: Phase is content-specific, not a learner trait
Phase boundaries are fuzzy and rarely measured directly
The synthesis draws on meta-analytic averages with heterogeneous quality
risks: Assigning a learner a permanent 'surface learner' label
Recommending transfer strategies before any knowledge exists
Treating the model as validated causal sequencing

observableEvidence.measure: Compare strategy effectiveness against a current-knowledge diagnostic
observableEvidence.caveat: An ineffective strategy may reflect wrong phase, not a bad strategy

evidence.basis: A synthesizing model over strategy meta-analyses; the phase interaction is plausible and useful but not established as a causal sequencing rule.
evidence.generalizability: Proposed as general; evidence is indirect.

recommendation.rationale: Good hypothesis generator for what to recommend next; must be tested against learner evidence, not assumed.

entries.label: Learning-styles matching
entries.summary: Do not classify learners into modality styles and match instruction to the preferred mode as a learning policy.
entries.mechanism: Preferences are real, but the claimed aptitude-by-treatment interaction needed to justify matching has not been demonstrated.
prerequisites: None; select representation by content, goal, and accessibility instead
constraints: Learner preferences can inform comfort or choice but not causal learning claims
risks: Stable labeling
Narrowing opportunities
Confusing accessibility needs with preferences
Misallocating design effort

observableEvidence.measure: Randomized comparison of matched and mismatched instruction with objective learning outcomes
observableEvidence.caveat: Preference surveys or main effects of one format do not test the meshing hypothesis

evidence.basis: Authoritative review found virtually no evidence meeting the required interaction standard and some contradictory results.
evidence.generalizability: The common meshing claim is unsupported across educational settings.

recommendation.rationale: Route by content affordance, current evidence, and accessibility—not a learner-style label.

entries.label: Learning trajectories
entries.summary: A learning trajectory pairs a goal with an empirically grounded developmental progression and matched instructional tasks for each level.
entries.mechanism: Knowing the typical next level lets an adult select a task just beyond the observed level rather than at an assumed grade level.
prerequisites: An empirically derived progression for the topic
Observation of the learner's current level
constraints: Progressions are typical paths, not required or universal ones
They exist for relatively few topics
Levels are inferred from behaviour, not measured directly
risks: Converting a trajectory into a fixed developmental gate
Treating an off-path learner as deficient
Assuming a trajectory validated in one population holds everywhere

observableEvidence.measure: Level-diagnostic tasks administered repeatedly with error analysis
observableEvidence.caveat: Level assignment is an inference and should be revisited

evidence.basis: Extensively developed and evaluated in early mathematics, and endorsed in evidence-rated early-mathematics guidance; coverage outside mathematics is thin.
evidence.generalizability: Strongest in early mathematics.

recommendation.rationale: Navigate from observed level rather than age, and keep the progression revisable rather than gating on it.

entries.label: Learning versus performance distinction
entries.summary: Performance during instruction is a poor and sometimes inverted proxy for durable learning, so evaluation must be delayed and transfer-oriented.
entries.mechanism: Current performance reflects momentary retrieval support and cueing; durable learning is a relatively permanent change observable when that support is withdrawn.
constraints: Requires deferred measurement, which costs time
Learners and instructors both misread fluency as mastery
risks: Optimizing a tutoring product for in-session success metrics
Declaring mastery from immediate post-tests
Removing effective practice because it looks inefficient

observableEvidence.indicator: Retention and transfer after support is removed
observableEvidence.measure: Delayed unassisted assessment and transfer items
observableEvidence.caveat: Immediate gains can vanish or reverse at delay

evidence.basis: Explicit review of decades of experiments showing dissociations between acquisition performance and retention or transfer.
evidence.generalizability: Broad across cognitive and motor domains.

recommendation.rationale: Treat as a measurement rule for any adaptive system: never let an in-session signal alone certify learning.

entries.label: Explicit phoneme-grapheme mapping
entries.summary: Explicitly connect speech segments to letters and practice blending, segmenting, decoding, and encoding.
entries.mechanism: Stable mappings between phonemes and graphemes support accurate decoding of unfamiliar words and spelling rather than contextual guessing.
prerequisites: Access to oral language in a known language
constraints: Pair code instruction with oral language, knowledge, fluency, and comprehension
Adapt for language and disability access
risks: Isolating oral phoneme drills indefinitely from print
Treating decoding as complete reading instruction
Guessing from pictures or context as a decoding substitute

observableEvidence.indicator: Accurate mapping and transfer to unfamiliar print
observableEvidence.measure: Segmentation, blending, letter-sound accuracy, pseudoword or unfamiliar-word reading, spelling, and error-type shift
observableEvidence.timing: Across cumulative lessons and on novel words
observableEvidence.caveat: Memorized word lists can mask weak decoding

evidence.basis: IES/WWC evidence-rated foundational-reading practice guide.
evidence.generalizability: Beginning readers and older learners with decoding gaps; language system and learner needs matter.

recommendation.rationale: Use explicit cumulative mapping when diagnostic evidence indicates an alphabetic decoding need.

entries.label: Mastery learning
entries.summary: Hold the criterion constant and let time vary: learners receive formative checks, corrective instruction, and re-assessment until a defined standard is met before moving on.
entries.mechanism: Frequent criterion checks plus targeted correctives prevent unremediated gaps from compounding into later failure.
prerequisites: Genuinely different corrective instruction, not just repetition
Flexible time and alternative assessment forms
constraints: Requires slack time, which fixed-pace systems rarely have
Effects shrink when correctives are only re-presentation
Criterion setting is a validity judgment, not a technical default
risks: Endless re-testing that becomes attrition by another name
Gaming the criterion with near-identical retest items
Fragmenting a subject into checkbox micro-objectives

observableEvidence.measure: Mastery rate, attempts to mastery, and delayed transfer performance
observableEvidence.caveat: Rising mastery rates can reflect easier retests

evidence.basis: Meta-analytic evidence of positive average effects, with strong dependence on corrective quality, criterion setting, and implementation.
evidence.generalizability: Strongest in hierarchical domains and in mastery-based professional training.

effect.note: Meta-analytic averages vary widely by implementation; treat as a range, not a constant.

recommendation.rationale: Strong fit for prerequisite-heavy content when correctives genuinely differ and the criterion is defensible.

entries.label: Mathematics and test anxiety
entries.summary: Anxiety consumes working memory during performance and produces avoidance over time; it is reciprocally related to achievement rather than simply caused by it.
entries.mechanism: Intrusive worry occupies the same limited working memory that the task needs, and avoidance reduces the practice that would build competence.
prerequisites: Measurement distinguishing anxiety from low competence
constraints: The relation is bidirectional; correcting only one side is insufficient
Effects are strongest for working-memory-intensive problems
Timed high-stakes formats amplify it
risks: Reading anxious underperformance as missing knowledge
Timed drills that entrench avoidance
Adults transmitting their own anxiety to learners

observableEvidence.indicator: Performance gap between anxious and low-pressure conditions
observableEvidence.measure: Same-content performance under timed and untimed conditions plus validated anxiety measures
observableEvidence.caveat: A single low score cannot distinguish anxiety from missing knowledge

evidence.basis: Consistent experimental evidence on working-memory interference plus a large meta-analysis establishing a robust negative association across ages.
evidence.generalizability: Broad, established from primary school through adulthood.

effect.note: Meta-analytic association between math anxiety and math achievement.

recommendation.rationale: Always consider anxiety as an alternative explanation for underperformance before inferring a knowledge gap.

entries.label: Mathematical strategy and error comparison
entries.summary: Compare correct, incomplete, or incorrect solutions and alternative strategies to make structural decisions and errors explicit.
entries.mechanism: Side-by-side comparison directs attention to when and why a method works and can build procedural flexibility and diagnostic reasoning.
prerequisites: Enough baseline knowledge to understand candidate strategies
constraints: Use active comparison rather than passive inspection
Match complexity to prior knowledge
risks: Mixed or negative effects for learners without baseline knowledge
Confusing exposure to an error with understanding it
Overloading novices with too many methods

observableEvidence.indicator: Flexible, justified method choice and error repair
observableEvidence.measure: Detect and correct error, generate another solution, select an efficient first step, justify choice, and transfer
observableEvidence.timing: After comparison and on a new problem
observableEvidence.caveat: Gains may appear in flexibility without uniform concept or procedure gains

evidence.basis: IES algebra guide rates multiple-strategy comparison moderate; solved-problem analysis evidence is minimal and mixed.
evidence.generalizability: Best after initial procedural footholds in algebra and related mathematics.

recommendation.rationale: Retrieve after diagnosing sufficient baseline knowledge and require explanation plus independent transfer.

entries.label: Systematic mathematical language and representation
entries.summary: Use explicit cumulative instruction to link precise mathematical language, quantities, selected visual or concrete models, and symbols.
entries.mechanism: Stable mappings among language, quantity, diagrams, and notation reduce ambiguity and build both conceptual and procedural access.
prerequisites: Diagnosis of the current mathematical bottleneck
constraints: Explain how each representation maps to the abstraction
Fade models when independent reasoning is ready
risks: Too many competing models
Manipulatives becoming procedures without meaning
Language demands hiding mathematical knowledge

observableEvidence.indicator: Conceptual and procedural mapping across forms
observableEvidence.measure: Explanation, translation among representations, procedural accuracy, and generalization
observableEvidence.timing: During intervention and on a novel representation
observableEvidence.caveat: Successful manipulation without explaining the mathematical relation is insufficient

evidence.basis: IES/WWC rates systematic instruction, mathematical language, and selected representations strongly for elementary intervention.
evidence.generalizability: Elementary learners struggling with mathematics; adapt model and language to content.

recommendation.rationale: Use a coherent representation system tied explicitly to language, symbols, and independent reasoning.

entries.label: Five strands of mathematical proficiency
aliases: conceptual understanding, procedural fluency, strategic competence, adaptive reasoning, productive disposition
entries.summary: Mathematical proficiency is an interwoven set of five strands, so a curriculum that develops only fluency or only understanding is incomplete by definition.
entries.mechanism: The strands are mutually dependent: strategic competence needs fluency to be feasible and understanding to be selective, and disposition governs whether either is exercised.
prerequisites: Assessment that can reach more than one strand
constraints: It is a consensus framework, not an intervention with an effect size
Strands are hard to assess separately
Productive disposition is rarely measured at all
risks: Claiming curricular quality from framework alignment
Assessing only the two easiest strands
Using it as a slogan rather than an audit tool

observableEvidence.measure: Assessment blueprint mapped to all five strands with evidence for each
observableEvidence.caveat: Alignment to a framework is not evidence of learning

evidence.basis: National Research Council consensus synthesis of mathematics learning; a definitional framework rather than a causal claim.
evidence.generalizability: Widely adopted in mathematics education policy and curriculum.

recommendation.rationale: Use as a coverage audit for mathematics goals and assessments, not as evidence of effectiveness.

entries.label: Metacognitive calibration and self-regulation
entries.summary: Teach learners to plan, monitor against evidence, select or change strategies, and evaluate outcomes.
entries.mechanism: More accurate monitoring supports better allocation of effort, strategy choice, and help seeking across a learning cycle.
prerequisites: Models and guided practice before independent regulation
constraints: Use delayed or performance-grounded judgments
Fade generic prompts when learners internalize the cycle
risks: Equating confidence with calibration
Generic reflection that adds load
Assuming novices can self-direct without knowledge

observableEvidence.measure: Predicted-versus-actual performance, logged strategy changes, help seeking, and delayed outcome
observableEvidence.timing: Before, during, and after a task
observableEvidence.caveat: Self-report alone does not establish regulation or learning

evidence.basis: Meta-analyses support explicit metacognitive strategy instruction, while transfer and prompt effects vary.
evidence.generalizability: Across school and adult learning, contingent on domain knowledge and explicit strategy instruction.

recommendation.rationale: Use concrete, domain-grounded cycles tied to objective evidence rather than free-form reflection.

entries.label: Monitoring accuracy and overconfidence
entries.summary: Learners are systematically overconfident about what they have learned, and the cues they use for judging learning are usually the wrong ones.
entries.mechanism: Judgments rely on processing fluency, which is inflated by rereading and by the presence of the material, so easy processing is misread as durable knowledge.
prerequisites: An external performance measure to calibrate against
constraints: Immediate judgments are strongly inflated; delayed judgments are far better
Learners resist strategies that feel harder despite better outcomes
Confidence ratings alone are not a learning measure
risks: Letting learners choose study strategies on felt fluency
Using self-rated understanding as a mastery signal
Reinforcing overconfidence with easy in-session success

observableEvidence.measure: Confidence judgments paired with delayed performance, reported as calibration error
observableEvidence.caveat: A confident learner can be the least accurate one

evidence.basis: A large replicated literature on judgment-of-learning inaccuracy and fluency-based misattribution.
evidence.generalizability: Robust across ages and materials studied.

recommendation.rationale: Never let self-rated understanding gate progression; ground monitoring in delayed external performance.

entries.label: Minimally guided instruction for novices
entries.summary: Instruction that withholds guidance while novices search for solutions is less effective than guided instruction, and can leave misconceptions unchallenged.
entries.mechanism: Novices lack the schemas that make search productive, so unguided problem solving consumes working memory on search rather than on learning.
prerequisites: None; this is a screening criterion
constraints: The critique targets minimal guidance, not inquiry or problem-based approaches that include guidance
Learners with high prior knowledge can benefit from reduced guidance
Deliberate short generation phases followed by instruction are a different and supported design
risks: Reading this as an argument against all inquiry
Reading the counterargument as licence to withhold guidance
Applying a single guidance level to all learners

observableEvidence.indicator: Guidance level recorded and matched to prior knowledge
observableEvidence.measure: Record what guidance was provided and analyse outcomes by prior-knowledge band
observableEvidence.caveat: Studies that do not report guidance level cannot settle this question

evidence.basis: A major critique supported by discovery-learning meta-analysis showing unassisted discovery underperforms explicit instruction, while enhanced and guided discovery outperform both.
evidence.generalizability: Robust for novices; the picture changes with expertise.

recommendation.rationale: Never withhold guidance from novices; make guidance level an explicit, recorded, prior-knowledge-dependent design decision.

entries.label: Montessori education
entries.summary: Classic Montessori shows some positive academic and social outcomes, but studies vary in quality and in how faithfully the method is implemented.
entries.mechanism: Child-chosen work with self-correcting materials in mixed-age classrooms is intended to combine agency with structured progression.
prerequisites: Fidelity to the classic materials and structure
constraints: Implementation varies enormously under an unprotected name
Selection effects are strong in non-randomized studies
Supplemented versions show weaker results than classic implementations
risks: Generalizing from lottery-based studies in atypical settings
Assuming the label guarantees the method
Ignoring access and cost inequities

observableEvidence.measure: Academic and social measures plus an implementation-fidelity audit
observableEvidence.caveat: Programme name alone tells you nothing about what happened

evidence.basis: A systematic review finds generally positive but heterogeneous evidence, with quality and fidelity limitations across studies.
evidence.generalizability: Preschool and primary; heavily dependent on implementation.

recommendation.rationale: Evaluate the specific implementation, not the label; require fidelity documentation before citing the evidence.

entries.label: Motivation through autonomy, competence, belonging, and purpose
entries.summary: Offer meaningful bounded choice, achievable challenge with structure, progress evidence, relational safety, and valued purpose.
entries.mechanism: Support for autonomy, competence, and relatedness can promote more autonomous regulation, engagement, and persistence.
constraints: Measure motivation and achievement separately
Attend to culture, identity, and context
risks: Equating autonomy with no guidance
Forced choice
Treating motivation as a fixed learner trait
Assuming engagement guarantees learning

observableEvidence.measure: Choice rationale, persistence, help seeking, need satisfaction, belonging, and objective performance
observableEvidence.timing: Across a sequence, not one task
observableEvidence.caveat: Self-reported enjoyment is a proximal outcome, not achievement

evidence.basis: Intervention meta-analysis and National Academies consensus support need-supportive design, with heterogeneous and sometimes nonsignificant outcomes.
evidence.generalizability: Across ages, but effects and culturally meaningful enactments vary.

recommendation.rationale: Combine choice with structure, feedback, belonging, and actual opportunities to build competence.

entries.label: Responsive intervention tiers (RTI/MTSS)
entries.summary: A tiered framework where universal instruction, targeted support, and intensive intervention are allocated by response data rather than by category labels.
entries.mechanism: Screening plus progress monitoring routes support by demonstrated need and response, allowing earlier intervention than referral-based models.
prerequisites: Strong universal instruction at tier one
Actual capacity to deliver intensive support
constraints: Weak tier-one instruction makes the whole system a referral pipeline
Implementation quality varies enormously
Using response data for disability identification remains technically contested
risks: Tiers used to delay evaluation and services
Disproportionate placement by group
Monitoring without changing instruction

observableEvidence.measure: Progress-monitoring response rates plus tier placement disaggregated by group
observableEvidence.caveat: Tier movement without instructional change indicates a process, not a support system

evidence.basis: A widely adopted framework with a substantial measurement base and ongoing technical debate about identification use.
evidence.generalizability: Mostly United States school systems.

recommendation.rationale: Only meaningful with strong universal instruction and real intervention capacity; audit placement for disproportionality.

entries.label: Programme models for multilingual learners
entries.summary: Multilingual learners benefit when their home language is treated as an asset and when academic content is not delayed for language acquisition.
entries.mechanism: Home-language knowledge transfers to the new language, and content learning and language learning develop together rather than sequentially.
prerequisites: Teachers prepared for integrated content and language work
Assessment in a language the learner can access
constraints: Programme model comparisons are confounded by implementation and policy
Language proficiency and content knowledge must be assessed separately
Local policy often constrains available models
risks: Delaying grade-level content until language is 'ready'
Misdiagnosing language barriers as learning disabilities
Treating multilingualism as a deficit

observableEvidence.indicator: Content learning and language growth, separately
observableEvidence.measure: Content assessment with language support plus separate language proficiency measures
observableEvidence.caveat: A single English-medium test confounds content knowledge with language proficiency

evidence.basis: National consensus reports on multilingual learners plus evidence-rated practice guidance for teaching academic content and literacy to English learners.
evidence.generalizability: Strongest evidence base is United States English-learner policy contexts.

recommendation.rationale: Keep content at grade level with language support, and never let an English-medium score stand as a content measure.

entries.label: Coherent multimedia and integrated representations
entries.summary: Combine words and relevant graphics when both serve the target relation, integrate references spatially or temporally, and remove seductive or redundant material.
entries.mechanism: Complementary representations can support selection, organization, and integration while coherent layout reduces avoidable search and split attention.
prerequisites: A target relation that benefits from depiction
Accessible alternatives for visual and auditory content
constraints: Representation choice must follow content and access needs, not a learner-style label
Signal relations explicitly
risks: Decorative media
Narrating identical dense on-screen text
Assuming more modalities always help

observableEvidence.measure: Explanation, diagram-text mapping, retention, transfer, and access-barrier report
observableEvidence.timing: After learning and on a novel representation
observableEvidence.caveat: Preference for a format is not evidence that it improves learning

evidence.basis: Evidence-rated institutional guidance supports graphics with verbal descriptions, with cognitive-load and accessibility boundary conditions.
evidence.generalizability: Strongest when visuals depict relevant structure and are coherently integrated.

recommendation.rationale: Use content-appropriate, coherent, accessible representations rather than modality matching.

entries.label: Cognitive theory of multimedia learning
